title: Cuts, abrasions and skin conditions at work
audience: Cleaning and support workers who handle body fluids, sharps, waste, linen or cleaning chemicals in healthcare settings.
learningOutcomes: Describe the sequence for covering a cut or abrasion before any further task.
Explain why an open wound changes which precautions apply.
State when a skin condition must be reported to the supervisor.

instruction.heading: Broken skin is an open route
instruction.body: A cut or abrasion gives microbes a route past the skin barrier. The guide names broken skin as both a portal of entry and a portal of exit (see “Where spread can be interrupted: the six links”). Cuts are difficult to prevent in cleaning work, even with careful work, so the question is how well a cut is covered and managed. Any open skin means more care with gloves, dressings and hand hygiene, and the protection should be checked before every task.

instruction.heading: Cover, glove and report
instruction.body: Follow your workplace policy for cuts. Wash the area using soap and water first and dry it. Cover it with a waterproof dressing, or with gauze or a sterile bandage if a waterproof one is not available. Gloves go on over the dressing before any further task. Tell your supervisor about the cut before the next task starts. Replace the dressing daily, and sooner if it becomes wet or soiled. Creams should be used only as your doctor directs for a skin condition. The guide points to hand creams with a water base that are listed on the ARTG, the TGA listing database; check that listing for the product you use.

instruction.heading: Skin conditions go to the supervisor
instruction.body: Any rash or other skin condition should be reported to your supervisor, who decides whether the condition limits the tasks you can do. Do not hide a rash because it seems minor, and do not decide for yourself that it is harmless. Do not diagnose it from pictures or from advice on the internet. Follow your employer policy on return to clinical contact, and keep the information private to those who need it.

instruction.heading: Keeping the skin working as a barrier
instruction.body: Warm water is kinder to the skin than hot water, and drying the hands fully with paper towel helps prevent cracking. Use hand rub where the procedure allows. Where you handle irritant chemicals, wear heavy-duty gloves, because a chemical burn or dry crack gives organisms an easier route in. The routine skin care in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits” applies to every shift.

procedure: Stop the task, wash the cut or abrasion using soap and water, and dry it.
Cover it with a waterproof dressing, or with gauze if none is available.
Wear single-use gloves over the dressing before any further task.
Tell your supervisor about the injury or skin condition before the next task starts.
Replace the dressing daily, or immediately if it becomes wet or soiled, and record the change if the facility requires it.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner cuts a finger on broken glass while clearing a room and a bin.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is done before the rest of the room is cleared?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. Wash the cut using soap and water, cover it with a waterproof dressing, and put on gloves. Pick up the glass with the approved method, and place sharp pieces in the sharps container (see “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”). Report the injury as an incident (see “Recording risks, hazard reports and breaches”).

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner has a red, weeping rash on the forearm and is asked to clean a ward kitchen.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop and tell the supervisor. The supervisor decides on the tasks that are safe, based on the policy and on the advice the worker receives. The cleaner does not decide alone and does not self-diagnose.

equipmentAndPpe: Soap and water, or a hand wash station
Waterproof dressings, gauze, or clean bandages
Disposable gloves in the correct size

commonErrors.error: Relying on a plaster alone and continuing without gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Cover the cut and wear gloves over the dressing before any task.

commonErrors.error: Not reporting a rash or cut because it seems small.
commonErrors.prevention: Tell the supervisor before the next task starts.

commonErrors.error: Using someone else cream or an unapproved product on a skin condition.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the product your doctor directs for you.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Deep, heavily bleeding or infected wounds need medical care. Follow first aid and the workplace procedure.
Check the ARTG listing for any hand cream before use.
Do not diagnose a skin condition. The supervisor and the employer decide on work limits.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner states the cover sequence in order, starting with washing the area.
Learner explains in their own words why broken skin changes the precautions.
Learner names the person to tell and the time to tell them about a skin condition.
documentationEvidence: Incident or injury record for the cut, with the time and the person told.
Record of dressing change if the facility requires it.
summary: Wash, cover, glove, then report before the next task.
Broken skin is both a route in and a route out for organisms.
A skin condition goes to the supervisor, who decides on work limits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has a cut on the hand. What should happen before the next task?
options: Keep working with a loose tissue on the cut and keep the glove off
Wash, cover with a waterproof dressing, wear gloves and tell the supervisor
Apply an alcohol rub only to the cut and the hand today and carry on
Wait for the cut to close on its own and keep working until then

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a cut be covered when a worker handles client equipment?
options: Because cuts are a way for organisms to enter the body
Because bandages make the cleaner look professional
Because cuts are not infection risks

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has a rash on the arm. What is the correct action?
options: Keep working, because rashes are not reportable
Apply a strong disinfectant to the rash
Tell the supervisor, who decides on work limits
Diagnose it by comparing it with online photos
